item.title: I replaced Samsung's app drawer with a custom launcher, and my Galaxy is finally usable
item.itunes:title: I replaced Samsung's app drawer with a custom launcher, and my Galaxy is finally usable
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I use an aging Samsung smartphone that’s almost four years old now. I bought it in 2022, and it's slowed down over time. Samsung’s Galaxy interface isn’t helping much either. I want to optimize the phone so it handles my regular daily functions easily, including finding the right app, switching between apps, and keeping them organized. Although I can add a bunch of apps to the home screen, too many make it hard to find anything. So I have to be selective, keeping four or five apps on the home screen and depending on Galaxy’s app drawer to find the rest.

I recently replaced the app drawer with a custom launcher, and before I get into the details, let me admit how thrilling it is to write about custom launchers in 2026. I’m using Niagara Launcher. If you’ve ever considered tweaking your phone’s interface, you’ve probably heard the name, and Niagara has made my Samsung Galaxy easier to use.

Samsung’s drawer still requires you to browse a grid of apps

I don't want to search for my apps

Samsung lets me sort apps alphabetically, group them into folders, or arrange them manually. I generally prefer alphabetical sorting because I don’t want to organize every app I install. That keeps the order predictable, though finding an app further down the drawer still means scrolling through rows of icons. You can use search, of course, but I don’t particularly want to bring up the keyboard every time I need an app that isn’t on my home screen.

Niagara gives my phone an alphabet along the edge of the screen. If I want to open Spotify, I can tap S and jump straight to that group. I can also slide my finger along the alphabet to move through the list. This has been really useful for apps I don’t open frequently enough to keep on the home screen. I only need to know the name, not which page or folder I put it in. For example, I don’t use Uber often enough to keep it on the home screen, but I still need it regularly. The same goes for my bank’s app and apps like Shazam or LinkedIn.

There’s also a small detail about Niagara’s sorting that I find very useful. It groups apps by their first letter, then puts frequently used apps higher within each group by default. You can disable this if you prefer strict alphabetical ordering.

Samsung already supports vertical scrolling in its drawer from One UI 7 onward, so you don’t need to switch launchers just to get that. The alphabet is the more useful addition for me because it gives me a direct way to reach a particular part of my app list.

I replaced my Google TV's home screen with a free launcher, and I don't want to go back

My new setup feels way more intuitive

12
By  Megan Ellis

Niagara gives my apps a simpler home

It's a lot easier to use

Niagara’s home screen gives your favorites the most attention. They appear in a vertical list, with their names beside their icons, so you don’t have to spread shortcuts across several pages to keep them accessible. The rest of your apps remain available through the alphabet. This is similar to how you can keep certain apps on the home screen in Samsung's default launcher, but I find Niagara's approach more convenient.

Niagara can also suggest frequently launched apps below your favorites. Its algorithm usually keeps the combined number of favorites and suggestions around eight, although it can show more when it identifies another frequently used app. You can dismiss individual suggestions or disable them altogether if you prefer choosing everything yourself.

Samsung also lets you build a sparse home screen. You can remove shortcuts, put apps into folders, and leave most of the screen empty. What I prefer about Niagara is that the launcher is already organized around a small selection of apps and direct access to the full list. I don’t have to decide how many pages to maintain or which folder should hold an app that doesn’t fit anywhere obvious.

I also love that Niagara Launcher lets me admire my wallpapers. I like to use a photo of my pets, my partner, or a picture I’ve taken as my phone’s wallpaper. Samsung’s launcher, apps, folders, and widgets cover a lot of it, and removing them means sacrificing functionality for aesthetics. Niagara lets me strike a perfect balance.

Its one-handed navigation is a meaningful difference

You can control everything with one hand

One reason I stick with this phone is that it’s small. It’s a Samsung Galaxy S21 FE, and they don’t make phones like this anymore, especially in the Android world and in this price range. I do use other Android phones occasionally, but I primarily stick to this one because I can comfortably reach every part of the screen with one hand. That’s a key deciding factor for me. Niagara makes one-handed navigation even easier by letting you use the alphabet from either screen edge. The alphabet is visible on the right, but you can also scroll along the left edge to access your apps.

Niagara lets you navigate by letter without opening the search field and typing. Whether you find it more comfortable depends on how you hold your phone, but I prefer having app navigation along the edge rather than reaching across several columns of icons.

Niagara also puts notification text beside the app that receives it. You can read a preview from the home screen, swipe right on the app to access its notifications and shortcuts, and reply through supported notifications.

The swipe-out pop-ups add another useful layer. They can contain shortcuts, related apps, and widgets, so you can keep extra functions close to an app without leaving everything permanently visible. For example, a calendar widget can sit inside a pop-up instead of occupying a large portion of the home screen.

You don’t get everything for free

While Niagara has some interesting features, not all of them are available for free. You get basic folders and app shortcut pop-ups at no cost, but if you want to add widgets to pop-ups, customize an app’s pop-up to hold other apps, or display full notifications inside pop-ups, you’ll need to pay for Niagara Pro. Niagara also lets you keep a calendar available on demand without it permanently sitting above your favorites. That’s one feature I don’t mind paying for in Niagara Pro.

4 launchers that turn my boring Pixel home screen into something actually useful

Give your Pixel a fresh look with these powerful launchers.

4

item.title: You're not alone: even the former CEO of Microsoft's advertising can't put the Windows 11 taskbar on the left yet
item.itunes:title: You're not alone: even the former CEO of Microsoft's advertising can't put the Windows 11 taskbar on the left yet
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • People still haven't gotten the ability to customize the taskbar on Windows 11.
  • Mikhail Parakhin installed 26H2, but found that taskbar customizations such as autohide and size controls aren't available to him yet.
  • The rollout is gradual; some users have the new taskbar options, while others must wait.

Listen, sometimes you have to fight for the freedom to do something, even if you yourself would never think of doing it. I'm a "taskbar at the bottom" kind of guy, and while I would never dream of having it on the left, I will advocate for the ability to put it there, simply because having the option is better than not having it.

Well, for all your left taskbar fans, you're in good company. An ex-CEO of Advertising for Microsoft has lamented that, despite updating to Windows 26H2, he still doesn't have the option to move the taskbar to the left.

If you don't have customizable taskbars yet, Mikhail Parakhin is right there with you

Here's hoping he gets the feature soon

As spotted by Windows Latest, Mikhail Parakhin took to X to post about his experience with the newly released Windows 11 26H2 update. Despite it installing just fine, Parakhin didn't get the taskbar feature, going so far as to say it's "not usable yet."

People in the replies pointed out that, while Windows 11 26H2 is generally available right now, not all of the features have completely rolled out. This includes the taskbar customization feature, which means some people can move the taskbar wherever they please, while others will be stuck with the old one for the time being. Still, it's good to hear that Microsoft is finally adding this much-wanted feature, even if I'd never use it myself.

Ex-Microsoft lead says he "fought hard" to save the vertical taskbar on Windows 11

I salute your efforts, sir.

2

item.title: I gave my Steam Deck a proper desktop mode with a dock and a mouse, and it replaced my travel laptop
item.itunes:title: I gave my Steam Deck a proper desktop mode with a dock and a mouse, and it replaced my travel laptop
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The Steam Deck is a powerful device, and I'm not talking about the frames it can push in AAA gaming at all, at least not here. I've previously argued that the Deck beats a budget gaming laptop on long-haul trips, and most of what I argued came down to the form factor, since the handheld was the clear winner in situations where I couldn't find a desk to house the laptop.

What's more to it, though, is that not only does the Deck keep me busy on an 8-hour-long flight, it also keeps me productive in the leg that follows it, in a way that's easier on the eyes, snappier for my workflow, and a little more grand for all of my entertainment needs. All it needs to do all of that is the addition of a dock that sells for $40. Here's why I think the Deck is better for my travel computing needs than my old Lenovo Legion 5 Pro.

An entire desktop setup can fit in my carry-on

A $40 dock, a mouse, a keyboard, and a portable monitor if I need it

Most of my travel setup can fit inside my carry-on. I have a 7-in-1 USB-C dock in there that cost me $40 on Amazon. It's considerably smaller than Valve's official dock, costs less than half as much, and offers a spec sheet that's better suited to my needs. With it, I can get 4K output at 60 Hz over HDMI, three USB-A 3.2 ports rated for 10Gbps, and 100W power delivery pass-through. I'm willing to bet that you could get a dock with similar specs for a similar or lower price online.

The rest of the kit consists of a Bluetooth mouse that conveniently comes with a 2.4GHz USB dongle, a slim wireless keyboard, and when the situation calls for it, a USB-C 1080p portable monitor. The Deck's 45W charger handles power through the dock as well, so there's no second power brick to pack. That's something I appreciate after years of hauling a 5-pound charger for my Lenovo Legion 5, which felt like it weighed as much as the Deck itself.

6 ways your Steam Deck can replace your laptop

You may be impressed by the many ways your Steam Deck can actually replace your laptop

3
By  Saeed Wazir

My hotel desk turns into a full office in less than a minute

SteamOS handles my browser tabs, Slack pings, and emails without complaint

Setting everything up is something that I'd argue takes perhaps less time than finding a comfortable spot for my bulky laptop (which needs to be conveniently placed next to a power outlet to last more than an hour). I can just drop the Deck into its dock, pull the portable monitor out, wake the keyboard, and plug the mouse's receiver into the dock. Within a moment, I'm looking at a rather comfortable desktop rather than the 7-inch screen.

Fascinatingly enough, I'd even go as far to say that Valve intended this exact use-case for SteamOS's Desktop Mode. The feature essentially enables me to access the Linux desktop that's complete with a taskbar, file manager, Firefox, and the Discover Software Center.

Now, one might argue that the lobby and conference room PCs that you can find in most hotels can do all of this too, but the problem is the friction associated with using them. They don't have my bookmarks, my signed-in sessions, or my Google Drive access.

My Steam Deck is a desktop for most of the week, and a dock was the only thing it needed

Handhelds are only as portable as you want them to be

2
By  Joe Rice-Jones

The Deck pulls off a trick my laptop never learned

Suspend a game on the big screen, resume it later on the smaller one

Once the workday is over, the Steam Deck can be what I primarily bought it for, which is a dedicated entertainment system. Because I can seamlessly switch back into Gaming Mode and have the entirety of my Steam library available on the hotel TV, it's easy to just kick back, pair whatever controller I packed, pair it over Bluetooth, and turn the setup into something that looks like my living room. Because I get to carry my browser data with it, Netflix and my YouTube accounts come with me, which means I don't have to type my login credentials into a hotel smart TV and remember to log out when I'm done.

There's also an underrated luxury that I have that I otherwise don't on my Legion laptop. Whenever a long gaming session concludes, I can press the power button, and the Deck will suspend the session instead of closing it.

The next morning, I can just pull it out of the dock, pack it into my bag, and pick up exactly where I left off on its display at the departure lounge. It's an effortless transition between the docked and handheld use that I've never managed with Windows, and it's one that makes owning the Deck a fluid, comprehensive experience rather than owning just another handheld gaming console.

It's shaped like a console, but it's as powerful as a PC

Most users who would purchase a Steam Deck would be led to believe that it's a gaming console, like a Nintendo Switch or the PSP, and sure enough, when I first purchased it, that's what I bought it for. However, over time, the Deck made me realize the difference between what a handheld gaming console and a handheld PC is. While the Deck is certainly shaped like it's designed for gaming, it's a device that can bear the weight of my workload on the road and still be the gaming handheld I bought when the work is done.

item.title: I cancelled Microsoft 365 for my family of five, and the hardest part was the hidden challenge I overlooked
item.itunes:title: I cancelled Microsoft 365 for my family of five, and the hardest part was the hidden challenge I overlooked
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Microsoft 365 had become a familiar part of our family's digital life, but I started wondering whether we really needed the entire package. With five people using different apps for different tasks, I wanted a setup that made more sense for how we actually worked. So I decided to explore alternatives instead of automatically renewing the subscription. I didn't expect every replacement to be perfect, but I wanted to see how far I could go without Microsoft's ecosystem. What surprised me most wasn't finding alternatives to its popular apps. It was discovering which part of the switch demanded the most effort.

OnlyOffice replaced office tools

Barely missed Microsoft Office

Replacing Word, Excel, and PowerPoint wasn't a big challenge for our family. We needed office apps for everyday tasks, like writing documents, managing spreadsheets, and putting together occasional presentations. OnlyOffice handled these tasks without making the switch feel complicated.

The biggest advantage was its familiar interface. Since it looks similar to Microsoft Office, my family didn't have to learn an entirely new way of working. The menus, formatting options, and overall layout felt familiar enough that everyone could get started without much guidance from me.

OnlyOffice also supports common Microsoft Office file formats, including DOCX, XLSX, and PPTX. This meant we could continue opening and editing our existing files without converting everything first. Whether someone needed to update a document or make a quick spreadsheet change, the process was straightforward.

Of course, OnlyOffice isn't a perfect replacement for every Microsoft Office feature. People who regularly use advanced Excel functions, complex document formatting, or specialized tools might notice some limitations. But for our family's everyday needs, those differences weren't a major concern.

What mattered most was that everyone could continue doing their usual office tasks without feeling that we had given up much. We didn't need every feature Microsoft offered; we needed tools that worked for the things we actually did.

Compared with the other parts of this migration, OnlyOffice was refreshingly simple. We could get back to our regular work without spending days adjusting to a new office suite.

I replaced Word, PowerPoint, Excel, OneDrive, and OneNote without paying Microsoft

Microsoft 365 without paying Microsoft

2
By  Parth Shah

Joplin took care of notes

A no-fuss home for notes

Notes were another part of our family's daily digital life that needed a new home. We wanted a simple way to keep track of lists, useful information, and everyday reminders without relying on Microsoft's apps. Joplin proved to be a practical choice.

We could create separate notebooks for different topics instead of keeping everything in one long list of notes. This made it easier to find things later, whether we were looking for a saved piece of information or checking something we had written down earlier.

Joplin also supports Markdown, but nobody in the family needed to learn it to get started with basic note-taking. Writing a quick note, creating a checklist, or organizing a few paragraphs required little effort. The interface was straightforward enough for everyday use.

Another advantage was that Joplin is open source and available across multiple platforms. That gave us flexibility in how we accessed our notes, without committing to another proprietary note-taking service. For our needs, though, Joplin did the job. We didn't need an elaborate note-management system. We needed a place to keep information organized and accessible, and Joplin was simple enough to fit into our routine without creating another learning curve.

Nextcloud replaced OneDrive

Family sharing turned out to be the hidden challenge

Replacing OneDrive with Nextcloud was where things got complicated. Unlike office apps, cloud storage needs to work quietly in the background. My family expected to save a file on one device and access it from another without thinking about how the process worked. Recreating that convenience with Nextcloud took more effort than I expected.

The initial setup wasn't the end of the job. I spent time configuring Nextcloud and getting it to work the way I wanted. There were more things to understand and manage than simply signing in to OneDrive and letting it sync files. Since I was setting this up for a family of five, I also had to think beyond my own account.

Family sharing turned out to be the hidden challenge. It wasn't enough for me to access my files successfully. Everyone needed a straightforward way to access their files and share what others needed. Managing accounts, permissions, and shared folders added another layer of work to the migration.

This was also where the difference between a cloud service and a self-hosted solution became obvious. Nextcloud gave me more control, but that control came with responsibility. I couldn't just assume everything would keep working without paying attention to the setup, updates, and backups.

I still liked the idea of having our files in a system I controlled. But getting Nextcloud to feel as effortless as OneDrive was harder than replacing Word or Excel. The software itself wasn't the main problem; making it work smoothly for everyone was.

I replaced Microsoft 365 with free open-source apps, but this one app is hard to leave behind

I thought leaving Microsoft 365 would mean endless compromises, but most replacements surprised me.

5
By  Yash Patel

We’re not going back to Microsoft 365

After moving our family to OnlyOffice, Joplin, and Nextcloud, I don't see us returning to Microsoft 365 anytime soon. The transition wasn't perfect, and getting Nextcloud to work the way we wanted took more effort than expected. But the experience helped me understand what our family actually needs from its software.

Not every family will want to manage a self-hosted setup, and that's perfectly fine. Microsoft's convenience is hard to ignore. For us, though, the extra effort is worth having more control over our tools and data. Word wasn't the problem. Replacing the convenience of the entire ecosystem was the real challenge.

item.title: I gave my retro DOS games the DLSS 5 treatment, and the results were all over the place
item.itunes:title: I gave my retro DOS games the DLSS 5 treatment, and the results were all over the place
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Ever since DLSS 5 dropped, I've been throwing it at any game that catches my fancy. I've "remastered" classic PS2 and PS3 games with DLSS 5, and AAA titles run pretty well with neural rendering despite my aging RTX 4070 Ti. In winding the clock back and remastering old games, I wondered what would happen if I threw DLSS 5's neural rendering layers on the pixelated worlds of some of the oldest games I'd ever played — my classic DOS collection.

Since these games came out well before modern graphics APIs and the hardware that supports them, I wasn't really expecting miracles. Still, between creative workarounds and a little experimentation, I managed to get DLSS 5 working on some of my favorite DOS-era classics.

DLSS 5 was never meant for games this old

Modern neural rendering pipelines don't play nice with DOS shooters

Getting DLSS 5 to work with games from the DOS era isn't quite as simple as pointing NVIDIA's neural rendering technology at an executable and hoping for the best. Modern graphics APIs didn't exist back then, so their rendering pipelines weren't designed with the kind of scene information that neural rendering requires — there are no motion vectors to read or latch on to. As such, I had to work around those limitations before I could even begin judging the results.

This is where my trusty method of using ReShade came in handy. OptiScaler is a pretty popular method of injecting DLSS 5 into a game, but it wouldn't have worked with games as old as Doom, Quake, or Blood. ReShade, on the other hand, uses DLSS 5's DLL files and applies a neural rendering overlay onto the game in real time.

I approached each game as a separate compatibility challenge, since DOSBox doesn't quite work well with a full-screen overlay like ReShade, either. Most importantly, though, getting DLSS 5 working would only be half the battle. I wasn't going to declare victory just because an AI-enhanced screenshot looked sharper. After all, retro DOS games have deliberately low-resolution textures, sprite-based enemies, and very carefully crafted visual identities.

Stop calling it AI slop — upscaling is democratizing high-end gaming for the 99%

Better visuals for those not on the bleeding edge.

26
By  Samarveer Singh

Doom and Doom II genuinely looked like remakes in some ways

DLSS 5 adds details to my classics, but also forgets what makes them iconic

I started with Doom and Doom II, two games with chunky sprites and muddy textures are as integral to their identity as the shotgun. With DLSS 5 enabled, the industrial corridors immediately gained much more convincing surface detail. The metallic panels became easier to distinguish, but the original sprite art did lose some of its deliberate crudeness.

The lighting difference with DLSS 5 was absolutely the biggest difference maker. The games took on a life of their own with DLSS 5's neural lighting, although it did take me three neural rendering passes to make the difference impressive. However, when it came to the enemies, doors, and other textures that have always been 2D sprites, DLSS 5 could make no difference at all. Doom's demons on Mars gained a bit more detail with more defined facial features (and abs), but even though DLSS 5 was changing the environment completely, the 2D sprites remained largely unchanged.

Doom II delivered similarly mixed results. Wall panels, ledges, and stonework looked more defined with DLSS 5, but the brighter presentation also changed the atmosphere, and considerably so. Some of these improvements were genuinely appealing, but to be fair, added detail isn't necessarily accurate detail.

I tested DLSS 5 on a DGX Spark, and it showed me the future is bright for Nvidia's first laptop

RTX Spark is going to be a game changer.

By  Rayan Malik

Blood made me want to turn off DLSS 5 immediately

It looks "modern," but at what cost?

The Doom games left me rather impressed with how they handled DLSS 5. The lighting, textures, and surfaces really did work to enhance the original game's feel, and the neural rendering acted as a remarkable fresh coat of paint. On the other hand, when I tried DLSS 5 with Blood, things changed considerably.

The original game relies heavily on a grimy and oppressive aesthetic. Stone walls and stony floors coated in blood, torches illuminating gory corners, and macabre lighting are what give Blood its iconic imagery and visual language. With DLSS 5, the crypts gained dramatic lighting, and the stone walls looked a lot more textured, with depth that the original presentation could never match. Unfortunately, the game lost all of its wonderfully grimy atmosphere in the process.

While DLSS 5's neural rendering passes never changed the enemy sprites in Doom, they transformed the ones in Blood. The pixelated sprites became disturbingly detailed human figures, with more defined clothes and musculature. They were possibly the only good thing to come out of the neural rendering transformation, but they were also complete AI interpretations of what those characters should look like, since the newly-added detail wasn't coming from the original assets.

Interiors in the game (which is pretty much 80% of the entire experience) suffered a rather concerning identity crisis. The textures became more pronounced, but the brighter lighting made the environments feel less oppressive. Blood is supposed to look filthy, sinister, and occasionally downright grotesque.

I can appreciate the technical wizardry involved, but I wouldn't want this treatment permanently enabled. When neural rendering starts rewriting a game's atmosphere and character designs, I would much rather keep the original pixels.

DLSS 5 made my retro games look remarkably different

But that never translated to objectively better

My experiments with Doom, Doom II, and Blood: Fresh Supply have left me with a rather complicated relationship with DLSS 5. The technology can dramatically improve environmental lighting and make decades-old textures appear more elaborate, but it also sometimes redesigns them from scratch.

Clearly, DLSS 5 doesn't always understand when to leave "good enough" alone. It ends up changing the character of pixelated, 2.5D games dramatically, and that makes sense, too, since the neural rendering tech was never made with 2.5D DOS-era games in mind. When it comes to genuinely retro games, DLSS 5 pretty much alters the qualities that make them memorable.

That doesn't mean I'm giving up on neural rendering for retro games. Quite the opposite. I'm fascinated by how far I can push it, but these experiments have convinced me that more detail isn't always an upgrade. If DLSS 5 wants to remaster my classics, it first needs to learn when to keep its hands off them.

I moved one thing in DLSS 5's pipeline, and it gave me back 50% of my frame rate

DLSS 5's transformative changes are so much more playable now

2
By  Samarveer Singh

Modern upscaling is all the remastering I need from my retro games

It's fascinating how DLSS 5 impressed me with its neural rendering all the way down to my PS1 games, but going back to last century's titles forced me to reconsider what I actually want from a remaster. I've spent years chasing sharper textures, better lighting, and higher resolutions, yet these experiments reminded me that technical improvements aren't worth much if they come at the expense of artistic intent.

I'd really rather have an ugly, authentic Baron of Hell than a photorealistic demon that looks like it wandered in from another game. If nothing else, my retro gaming backlog has taught me that sometimes, nostalgia doesn't need an AI makeover.

With DLSS 5 enabled, the industrial corridors immediately gained much more convincing surface detail. The metallic panels became easier to distinguish, but the original sprite art did lose some of its deliberate crudeness.

The lighting difference with DLSS 5 was absolutely the biggest difference maker. The games took on a life of their own with DLSS 5's neural lighting, although it did take me three neural rendering passes to make the difference impressive. However, when it came to the enemies, doors, and other textures that have always been 2D sprites, DLSS 5 could make no difference at all. It looks "modern," but at what cost?

Interiors in the game (which is pretty much 80% of the entire experience) suffered a rather concerning identity crisis. The textures became more pronounced, but the brighter lighting made the environments feel less oppressive. Blood is supposed to look filthy, sinister, and occasionally downright grotesque.

I can appreciate the technical wizardry involved, but I wouldn't want this treatment permanently enabled. When neural rendering starts rewriting a game's atmosphere and character designs, I would much rather keep the original pixels.

But that never translated to objectively better

My experiments with Doom, Doom II, and Blood: Fresh Supply have left me with a rather complicated relationship with DLSS 5. The technology can dramatically improve environmental lighting and make decades-old textures appear more elaborate, but it also sometimes redesigns them from scratch.

Clearly, DLSS 5 doesn't always understand when to leave "good enough" alone. It ends up changing the character of pixelated, 2.5D games dramatically, and that makes sense, too, since the neural rendering tech was never made with 2.5D DOS-era games in mind. When it comes to genuinely retro games, DLSS 5 pretty much alters the qualities that make them memorable.

That doesn't mean I'm giving up on neural rendering for retro games. Quite the opposite. I'm fascinated by how far I can push it, but these experiments have convinced me that more detail isn't always an upgrade. If DLSS 5 wants to remaster my classics, it first needs to learn when to keep its hands off them.

I moved one thing in DLSS 5's pipeline, and it gave me back 50% of my frame rate

DLSS 5's transformative changes are so much more playable now

2
By  Samarveer Singh

Modern upscaling is all the remastering I need from my retro games

It's fascinating how DLSS 5 impressed me with its neural rendering all the way down to my PS1 games, but going back to last century's titles forced me to reconsider what I actually want from a remaster. I've spent years chasing sharper textures, better lighting, and higher resolutions, yet these experiments reminded me that technical improvements aren't worth much if they come at the expense of artistic intent.

I'd really rather have an ugly, authentic Baron of Hell than a photorealistic demon that looks like it wandered in from another game. If nothing else, my retro gaming backlog has taught me that sometimes, nostalgia doesn't need an AI makeover.

item.title: Obsidian's plugin library doubled to over 8,000 this year, and you still only need about four of them
item.itunes:title: Obsidian's plugin library doubled to over 8,000 this year, and you still only need about four of them
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Obsidian has grown in popularity, and the plugin library has absolutely exploded. It's grown by more than 3,000 plugins in the last few months alone, with options for nearly every niche or application you can think of. It's impressive, and it's always fun to browse the library to see what's new. But here's the thing: despite the plugin library's exponential growth, you really only need a few. By all means, install as many as you want — but if you're minimizing your vault, these are the four I'd keep.

Templater and Dataview

Two of the most powerful plugins in the library

If I had to choose only two plugins, I'd install Templater and Dataview. Templater is a must-have for creating templates for recurring note types. I use one for all my Substack articles, and it automatically creates fields for the tags and properties I need. Templater expands on Obsidian's core Template plugin with a wide range of features and compatibility with dynamic content.

I also use a template for my daily notes, and it works with Dataview to pull information about my day straight into the note. The two plugins each have a different job, but they work incredibly well together. Templater gives each daily note a set, predictable layout, while Dataview searches the vault and compiles information. Depending on how you use your vault, that can mean pulling a task list, related notes, or other details into a single spot for easy review.

I can’t use Obsidian without changing these 8 settings first

Don’t touch your vault without tweaking these Obsidian settings

3
By  Parth Shah

Excalidraw

For visual thinking

Excalidraw is the most-downloaded plugin in the Obsidian community library, and for good reason. Excalidraw users are offered an easy integration into the Obsidian ecosystem, and many other users — myself included — discovered Excalidraw through Obsidian. The app is useful for everything from quick sketches to brainstorming, and it even works for things you might not expect, like dealing with maps. That last application has been a godsend for my fantasy-novel vaults.

Style Settings

Because what's a vault without customization?

Obsidian has many themes to choose from, and while most look great out of the box, deeper customization requires the Style Settings app to tweak things the way you want. The level of customization available depends on the theme. For one of my vaults, I use the Typewriter theme, which offers minimal settings (although it does grant easy access to the CSS for theme-wide changes). My primary vault uses AnuPpuccin, and it leans heavily on Style Settings for granular customization.

It offers subsettings for everything from the vault's overall color, including specific choices for light and dark mode themes, to color settings for callouts, tables, and more. There are too many settings; for the most part, I've stuck with the defaults. The number of options available for AnuPpuccin is a bit overwhelming, but for users who like to get into the finest details of their vault's appearance, it's one you don't want to miss.

I turned Obsidian into a personal command center, and now I barely open separate apps

My notes, tasks, calendar, research, and writing finally live under one roof.

5
By  Patrick Hearn

There are no "universal" plugins

The best options for you depend entirely on how you use your vault

When I started writing this, I tried to pick out plugins that would apply to the widest range of users. It felt natural to go with the most downloaded; after all, those are the most common choices by default. That said, even these aren't always applicable. If you don't work with large data sets, then Dataview might not be the most useful tool. If you use Obsidian more as a second brain to store articles and things you find interesting rather than as a note-taking platform, you might not find much use for Templater. That's the magic of Obsidian: there are as many ways to use the app as there are users, but it also makes it tough to find the best overall plugins.

For example, I rely on StoryLine for all of my fiction-focused vaults. It's an incredible tool for keeping complicated plotlines organized and making it easy to reference earlier events, but if you aren't a writer, it's not useful for much else (though I think it would work well as a TTRPG management tool). If you're just starting out in Obsidian and want to install plugins, I'd caution you to wait, figure out how you actually use your vault, and then search for plugins that fit your workflow rather than trying to build a workflow around the plugins.

More plugins is a win, but be selective

Too many plugins can slow your vault, especially if you use Obsidian primarily on mobile. My main vault has more than 30 plugins, and I definitely see a performance impact compared to some of my secondary vaults that have fewer than ten.

item.title: I put my Zigbee coordinator on a USB extension cable, and half my flaky sensors started working
item.itunes:title: I put my Zigbee coordinator on a USB extension cable, and half my flaky sensors started working
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The universal frustration of smart home deployment is when things stop working. Some of your buttons stop responding, door sensors report unavailable, and motion triggers take 10 seconds to fire even though your mesh looks fine on paper. It's easy to blame bad routing, cheap sensors, or weak batteries, and you'll end up ripping your hair out trying to repair devices or shuffle routers around the house.

But the actual source of the chaos might not be your devices at all. It could be electromagnetic radiation bleeding directly out of the USB 3.0 port where your coordinator is plugged in. You don't need a more expensive Zigbee dongle or a hardware reset. By simply moving your coordinator away from the noisy electromagnetic soup of your mini PC or server using a cheap USB 2.0 extension cable, you can instantly resurrect your flaky sensors.

Your neighbors' Wi-Fi is slowing yours down, and one simple setting can fix it

Your router's default wireless channel may not be the most optimal

4
By  Tanveer Singh

USB 3.0 interference can be a nightmare

Understanding the interference can help you avoid it

  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons

USB 3.0 interference creates a 2.4GHz electromagnetic nightmare. This means that when you plug a 2.4GHz radio directly into a modern computer port, it can create a whole lot of issues without you even realizing what the problem is.

The 2.4GHz spectrum has a lot of overlap. Both USB 3.0 data lines and the Zigbee/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth protocols operate in or near the 2.4GHz ISM band. That means that so many different devices and protocols can all interfere with one another. When you're plugging your Zigbee USB dongle into something like a mini PC that utilizes all of these protocols, there is so much interference around the device itself.

Alongside this, there can also be the issue of unshielded or poorly grounded USB 3.0 ports, which can emit broadband electromagnetic noise right around 2.4GHz. When a Zigbee coordinator is plugged directly into a mini PC, Raspberry Pi 4/5, or server chassis, that local radiation deafens the radio's receiver, drowning out weak packets from distant sensors.

The fix is simple

A cheap extension cable can make a major difference

Luckily, a USB extension cable can fix this problem. This can cost a couple of dollars and make a major difference to your smart home's connectivity and performance. This old-school physical workaround outperforms expensive hardware upgrades for two simple reasons.

The first is spatial isolation. Moving the coordinator even just three feet away from the server chassis places it outside the immediate high-intensity electromagnetic radiation bubble of the USB 3.0 ports and internal power supplies. Essentially, by giving your dongle enough room, you're moving it away from the high levels of interference.

However, when you're purchasing your USB extension cable, you should explicitly use a USB 2.0 extension cable or plug the cable itself into a USB 2.0 port if it's available. This is because USB 3.0 cables add extra high-speed data pairs that can radiate more noise if poorly shielded, whereas a standard USB 2.0 extension cable lacks these noisy high-frequency data lines while providing more than enough bandwidth for a serial Zigbee radio.

Don't let Wi-Fi be your downfall

Secondary interference can cause problems too

When picking up a USB extension cable, not only can you move your dongle away from the PC that could be causing interference issues, but it also allows you to reposition your dongle away from Wi-Fi channel congestion. There is a whole lot of secondary 2.4GHz interference sources within your home too.

Even with an extension cable, if your Zigbee controller is sitting directly next to a Wi-Fi access point operating on overlapping 2.4GHz channels (like Wi-Fi channels 1, 6, or 11 versus Zigbee channels 11, 15, 20, or 25), you can still experience interference. Ensure that you reposition your dongle somewhere adequately away from both your smart home mini PC and your router or mesh node.

Alongside this, you can also implement a coexistence strategy. You can ensure your home Wi-Fi uses a fixed 20MHz width on 2.4GHz, and your Zigbee network is cleanly pinned to a non-overlapping channel, such as channel 15, 20, or 25. This should hopefully rid you of some of the interference, as even though the 2.4GHz channel is being used, the different widths keep them apart.

The bottleneck might not be your hardware

Save yourself the cash

Sometimes it's really easy to overcomplicate home lab troubleshooting by rewriting configs, chasing firmware, or replacing hardware, but sometimes the real bottleneck is simple physics. If your Zigbee network is driving you mad, it might be better for you to pull out your coordinator and get it away from that USB 3.0 port. Put it on an extension cable and your smart home might finally settle down. Just ensure that you're not moving it in the way of secondary interference within your home. This fix can save you a whole load of cash in time spent troubleshooting and hardware upgrades you might not need.

The universal frustration of smart home deployment is when things stop working. Some of your buttons stop responding, door sensors report unavailable, and motion triggers take 10 seconds to fire even though your mesh looks fine on paper. It's easy to blame bad routing, cheap sensors, or weak batteries, and you'll end up ripping your hair out trying to repair devices or shuffle routers around the house.

But the actual source of the chaos might not be your devices at all. It could be electromagnetic radiation bleeding directly out of the USB 3.0 port where your coordinator is plugged in. You don't need a more expensive Zigbee dongle or a hardware reset. By simply moving your coordinator away from the noisy electromagnetic soup of your mini PC or server using a cheap USB 2.0 extension cable, you can instantly resurrect your flaky sensors.

Your neighbors' Wi-Fi is slowing yours down, and one simple setting can fix it

Your router's default wireless channel may not be the most optimal

4
By  Tanveer Singh

USB 3.0 interference can be a nightmare

Understanding the interference can help you avoid it

  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons

USB 3.0 interference creates a 2.4GHz electromagnetic nightmare. This means that when you plug a 2.4GHz radio directly into a modern computer port, it can create a whole lot of issues without you even realizing what the problem is.

The 2.4GHz spectrum has a lot of overlap. Both USB 3.0 data lines and the Zigbee/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth protocols operate in or near the 2.4GHz ISM band. That means that so many different devices and protocols can all interfere with one another. When you're plugging your Zigbee USB dongle into something like a mini PC that utilizes all of these protocols, there is so much interference around the device itself.

Alongside this, there can also be the issue of unshielded or poorly grounded USB 3.0 ports, which can emit broadband electromagnetic noise right around 2.4GHz. When a Zigbee coordinator is plugged directly into a mini PC, Raspberry Pi 4/5, or server chassis, that local radiation deafens the radio's receiver, drowning out weak packets from distant sensors.

The fix is simple

A cheap extension cable can make a major difference

Luckily, a USB extension cable can fix this problem. This can cost a couple of dollars and make a major difference to your smart home's connectivity and performance. This old-school physical workaround outperforms expensive hardware upgrades for two simple reasons.

The first is spatial isolation. Moving the coordinator even just three feet away from the server chassis places it outside the immediate high-intensity electromagnetic radiation bubble of the USB 3.0 ports and internal power supplies. Essentially, by giving your dongle enough room, you're moving it away from the high levels of interference.

However, when you're purchasing your USB extension cable, you should explicitly use a USB 2.0 extension cable or plug the cable itself into a USB 2.0 port if it's available. This is because USB 3.0 cables add extra high-speed data pairs that can radiate more noise if poorly shielded, whereas a standard USB 2.0 extension cable lacks these noisy high-frequency data lines while providing more than enough bandwidth for a serial Zigbee radio.

Secondary interference can cause problems too

When picking up a USB extension cable, not only can you move your dongle away from the PC that could be causing interference issues, but it also allows you to reposition your dongle away from Wi-Fi channel congestion. There is a whole lot of secondary 2.4GHz interference sources within your home too.

Even with an extension cable, if your Zigbee controller is sitting directly next to a Wi-Fi access point operating on overlapping 2.4GHz channels (like Wi-Fi channels 1, 6, or 11 versus Zigbee channels 11, 15, 20, or 25), you can still experience interference. Ensure that you reposition your dongle somewhere adequately away from both your smart home mini PC and your router or mesh node.

Alongside this, you can also implement a coexistence strategy. You can ensure your home Wi-Fi uses a fixed 20MHz width on 2.4GHz, and your Zigbee network is cleanly pinned to a non-overlapping channel, such as channel 15, 20, or 25. This should hopefully rid you of some of the interference, as even though the 2.4GHz channel is being used, the different widths keep them apart.

The bottleneck might not be your hardware

Save yourself the cash

Sometimes it's really easy to overcomplicate home lab troubleshooting by rewriting configs, chasing firmware, or replacing hardware, but sometimes the real bottleneck is simple physics. If your Zigbee network is driving you mad, it might be better for you to pull out your coordinator and get it away from that USB 3.0 port. Put it on an extension cable and your smart home might finally settle down. Just ensure that you're not moving it in the way of secondary interference within your home. This fix can save you a whole load of cash in time spent troubleshooting and hardware upgrades you might not need.

item.title: The new GNOME OS Preview is perfect for people who want something more stable than nightly
item.itunes:title: The new GNOME OS Preview is perfect for people who want something more stable than nightly
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • GNOME OS was only available as nightly builds, which limited its appeal to non-developers.
  • GNOME OS Preview bridges nightly and stable, offering newer features with improved daily reliability.
  • Stable GNOME OS is planned but needs work on systemd-homed, TPM, ARM support, and a feature-rich installer.

I really love bleeding-edge Linux distros. Sure, they may not be the most stable distros of the bunch, but I love getting the newest features first. Regardless, I totally understand why people would shy away from something like GNOME OS, which, until now, only had a nightly build. Now, the GNOME Foundation has announced GNOME OS Preview, which takes a comfy middle ground between receiving the newest features and having a stable system.

GNOME OS Preview brings the newest in GNOME to those who dislike nightly builds

Hopefully, a more stable GNOME OS version will arrive soon

As described by Adrian Vovk on his blog, this new version of GNOME OS aims to be more suited to regular use. While I'm sure anyone who loves nightly build distros would be comfortable with the current offering, Vovk was worried that it wasn't suited for the rest of us:

"Even though GNOME OS has been usable on real hardware for a few years now, its appeal was limited. We’ve only had the Nightly edition, which is constantly rebuilt to ship the latest git commit of every GNOME component (and a few others, like systemd and Flatpak). This form of GNOME OS is extremely useful, since GNOME developers and designers can daily-drive it to test the latest changes. However, it’s not something we’d recommend to non-developers."

The obvious solution is to release GNOME OS Stable, but as Vovk mentions, there are still a few issues he wants ironed out before it's ready for the red carpet. For instance, he'd prefer that the OS had proper integration for systemd-homed, better integration with TPM, better support for Arm hardware, and a feature-rich installer, to name a few.

As such, to patch that gap between a nightly build and a stable one, Vovk announced GNOME OS Preview. While it's not as stable as it could be, Vovk is confident that this version will be "reliable enough for daily use by non-developer enthusiasts," which gives something regular people can actually use until GNOME OS Stable is released. Honestly, I'm a little tempted to try it myself, and I'm a KDE fanboy.

If you'd like to give it a spin, pop over to the GNOME download page, scroll down a little, and click the button underneath the "Preview" label.

item.title: Intel's 12th Gen CPUs have become the Windows 10 of PC hardware, and nobody is in a hurry to leave
item.itunes:title: Intel's 12th Gen CPUs have become the Windows 10 of PC hardware, and nobody is in a hurry to leave
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Are you still using Windows 10? There's a 27% chance that you are, which is surprising, considering Windows 11 has been out for over five years. In fact, it's been over a year since Microsoft ended support for Windows 10. Despite that, people refuse to abandon the beloved OS in favor of Windows 11 for a variety of reasons. Similarly, Intel's 12th Gen (Alder Lake) owners aren't motivated to upgrade to something else.

CPUs like the Core i5-12400, Core i5-12600K, and Core i7-12700K are still beloved chips, providing more than enough gaming performance. High-end SKUs like the Core i9-12900K pack productivity chops as well, convincing users to retain their CPUs for a few more years. With the 13th and 14th Gen CPUs mired in controversy and a platform upgrade inaccessible to most people, the 12th Gen series is here to stay.

6 "old" CPUs worth buying in 2026 because they work with the RAM you already own

Don't waste money on inflated DDR5 systems

By  Tanveer Singh

12th Gen CPUs are far from old in 2026

Users are still getting their money's worth

Credit: Wikimedia Commons

We know how the majority of PC users love to retain their CPUs for 5–7 years, and some users stretch that to even 10 years. This is because the definition of "old CPUs" has changed considerably in recent years. A processor launched in 2021 didn't become outdated in 2026, unlike 2016's 6th Gen chips that were nowhere to be found five years later.

Intel's 12th Gen CPUs debuted a brand-new hybrid core architecture and breathed new life into Team Blue's lineup. The Performance and Efficiency cores not only provided great performance but also excelled in terms of power efficiency. Five years later, CPUs like the Core i5-12400 and Core i5-12600K are still perfectly capable of 1080p and 1440p gaming. Modern chips are faster, but it's not a gigantic difference.

Moreover, 12th Gen owners aren't losing out on any major platform-related features. PCIe 5.0 and DDR5 support (on the right motherboard) are available, and so is Resizable BAR. If you happen to own a Core i9-12900K, you can even run many productivity workloads without losing out on much. We've seen Intel launch four generations of CPUs after Alder Lake, but it's still just a 5-year-old chip, and most users are still getting what they want out of it.

6 CPUs that are officially too old in 2026

It might be the end of the line for your trusty ol' CPU

27
By  Tanveer Singh

They don't have the baggage of Intel's 13th and 14th Gen chips

The 12th Gen is stable, to say the least

In case you didn't know, Intel's 13th and 14th Gen came under fire for a "Vmin shift instability" bug over two years ago. This was a hardware defect affecting these two CPU generations, which sent excessive voltage to the chips, leading to irreversible silicon degradation. Intel eventually released microcode updates to fix the issues, but the CPUs already affected by the bug had already suffered lasting damage.

Hence, 12th Gen owners thinking of switching to a pre-owned 13th or 14th Gen CPU on the same motherboard have a huge reason to reconsider. Intel didn't handle the crisis as well as it could have, and its reputation took a severe hit. AMD naturally benefited from it, not that Team Red wasn't doing great work on its own.

The 12th Gen chips are, therefore, the last "safe" generation of chips on the LGA 1700 platform. Existing owners don't have enough to gain, performance or otherwise, so upgrading to a 13th or 14th Gen chip isn't the default choice that it could have been.

5 reasons to avoid Intel's desktop CPUs right now

Intel is in a bad place right now, and it's best to steer clear of Arrow Lake and Raptor Lake for your desktop PC

20
By  Tanveer Singh

A platform upgrade in this market has never been more difficult

There's no light at the end of the tunnel

Moving to a 13th or 14th Gen CPU may not be ideal, but what about a platform upgrade to Arrow Lake? Well, even that's easier said than done. Ever since the DRAM crisis skyrocketed consumer memory prices last year, upgrading to a DDR5 system went from pricey to downright impossible. Today, a typical 32GB kit of DDR5-6000 RAM costs at least $480, a fourfold increase compared to just 12 months ago. Even DDR4 RAM isn't immune to the price hikes.

When there's little to gain from a platform upgrade for gamers and regular users, what's the point of overspending? 12th Gen owners are ready to wait it out. Even if the crisis lasts longer than expected, Alder Lake CPUs aren't getting outdated anytime soon. Gamers have always held on to their CPUs far longer than their GPUs anyway. And with GPU prices also in the stratosphere, it's natural to allocate all your budget to a new graphics card instead.

With GPU prices climbing, a 1080p high-refresh rate monitor is the budget gaming sweet spot

GPUs capable of 1440p at high-refresh rates have become a luxury

1
By  Ty Sherback

For many, the 12th Gen series was the last good lineup Intel launched

It's been five years since Alder Lake came out, but Intel users are still waiting for a generation good enough to upgrade to. The PC hardware prices haven't helped, but it's also true that 12th Gen CPUs are still going strong. Whether it's gaming, productivity, or stability, 12th Gen owners have enough reasons to retain their CPU for a few more years.

item.title: I put all of Wikipedia on my home server, and it still answers when the internet is down
item.itunes:title: I put all of Wikipedia on my home server, and it still answers when the internet is down
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
We live in an age where getting any kind of information can be done in a few minutes with a simple internet search. But that's just the thing — all that information lives on the internet, so you're always dependent on a connection to get the answers you need, even if you have a locally hosted LLM to ask questions.

I wanted an answer system that could work even if my internet was down, so I built it. I downloaded Wikipedia and self-hosted it using Kiwix, and now I have all the information I could want right inside my house.

Hosting Wikipedia isn't as hard as I thought

It can be a big download, but still

With how massive of a resource Wikipedia can be, you'd be forgiven for thinking you can't fit it on your own computer. But it turns out you can, and all it takes is the right self-hosted service: Kiwix.

I deployed Kiwix in my Proxmox home lab using the respective community script, only increasing the disk size to 10GB from the default 4GB to accommodate the size of the Wikipedia database I was planning to download. You can download a wide range of variants of the Wikipedia database, even if you're strictly looking to keep every article in English.

The full list of databases is here, if you're curious, and you can download your choice by going into the container's terminal and navigating to its data folder, then use wget to pull the file you want from that list.

With just a Raspberry Pi, you can host your own offline Wikipedia: here's how I did it

This is such an easy project that the most time-consuming, difficult aspect was deciding just how much of Wikipedia's content I wanted to self-host.

2
By  Jeff Butts

To fit the relatively small container, I downloaded the Simple English version of Wikipedia, and I specifically went for the nopic variant, which doesn't include any images from articles, either. This database comes to a little over 1GB, so it can easily fit on any computer. I was tempted to go for the standard English database that would have been around 50GB, but I decided against it, mostly for time reasons.

What Kiwix actually looks like

It's exactly what you'd expect

With the database downloaded and Kiwix rebooted to load it, I now have a tons of information available at my fingertips. Any database I choose to download is shown as a separate "book", so I could reasonably have multiple variants here, whether I want to focus on specific areas of study or to have different language variants of Wikipedia.

The Simple English version of Wikipedia may not have quite as much information, but I can look up Paul Rudd and see a list of the movies he's worked on, and that's already very cool. In fact, I can look up almost anything and get a relatively basic overview of that topic or person. Pages look basically just like they would on the internet version of Wikipedia, and links are preserved, too.

This self-hosted Wikipedia is wrong about everything, and it's hilarious

This vibe coded abomination is one of the funniest things I've installed all year

5
By  Joe Rice-Jones

While the Wikipedia pages are viewable without internet, the included links naturally require an online connection, but it's still great to have them here. I can see the most important information offline, and if I need to check sources, I can still do it easily if I do have an internet connection.

Getting it to answer my questions

That's another challenge entirely

Now that I had my personal Wikipedia up and running, I wanted to see if I could ask it questions using natural language. This took a bit of work. First, I had to set up an MCP server that can query Kiwix, and I went with this one. There are others that can interact with the ZIM archives Kiwix relies on, though. I actually had to fix the main build file for this one, as it declares a "capabilities" parameter that doesn't seem to exist. After removing that specific portion from the main.ts file, I was able to use npm to build the MCP server and start running it.

Then, I had to use llama.cpp to download an LLM to use offline. I went with Qwen3.8-27B. I initially tried a distilled 4B version of this model, but I was getting a lot of incorrect information, so I had to step up to a more powerful model and hardware. I decided to run this part of the setup on a Minisforum AI X1 Pro review unit I had lying around, which has an AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 processor and 64GB of DDR5 RAM.

I connected Google Antigravity to Figma with MCP, and it turns my designs into working code in minutes

The design-to-code handoff meeting might be over

1
By  Nolen Jonker

Finally, I needed an agent harness to connect the MCP and the LLM so I could ask natural language questions. I installed Pi, added the MCP server to the configuration, and then connected it to the llama.cpp model I had on the machine. One particular setting I had to change within Pi was to change the MCP server exposure from the default codemode to direct. Otherwise, Pi seemed to bypass the MCP server when I asked any questions.

With all this finally done, I was able to ask Pi questions about these articles, and it was actually querying my Kiwix server to get answers without connecting to the internet. It does take a few minutes to get me answers, though.

It's (mostly) accurate

Results can be hit or miss for longer pages

While I was able to get this to work, I did notice some issues when trying to set this up, which may have contributed to why I needed a 27-billion-parameter model to get usable answers in the first place. When calling the tools enabled by the MCP server, I noticed the target content was parsed as plain text with all the HTML tags, which were then crudely stripped in the following step, potentially wasting tokens and resulting in a worse job extracting information.

That may be why using a 4-billion-parameter model resulted in gibberish answers. When I asked "Who is Paul Rudd?", while it got basic details like his name and birthday right, the filmography was completely made up.

Upgrading to a 27-billion-parameter model, I was able to get much closer to reality, but still not perfect. It got most of the details about Paul Rudd's filmography right, except it claimed his character's name in the Marvel Cinematic Universe is Pete Peterson (it should be Scott Lang) and made up a movie called Down and Out with the Ducks. Interestingly, these errors weren't repeated on a second run of the query.

I don’t pay for Perplexity or ChatGPT after combining my local LLMs with Perplexica and SearXNG

It's a neat way to avoid outdated responses to my queries

5
By  Ayush Pande

I also asked it "What is the Nintendo Switch 2?", and in this case, the response pretty much completely accurate. It told me the exact reveal and launch date in the US, it highlighted all they key specs accurately, and even included some information about early titles on the platform, all of which were accurate. It mentioned that the console launched on August 8 in Canada, but after checking Kiwix, it seems like that information was wrong in the Wikipedia database, too, so it's not a problem with the model.

The big difference between the two is the size of the page, and the fact that Paul Rudd's page on the Simple English Wikipedia has a fairly long table. The HTML tags for it may have taken a significant chunk of tokens while processing the request and hurt the quality of the output as it scanned further down the page.

It's still amazing

Even if the responses I get from my LLM aren't 100% accurate to the information on Kiwix, this entire process is kind of amazing. Simply having my own Wikipedia that I can use offline is already very cool, but it's made even better when I can set up a local LLM to query that database and answer questions for me, all without going to the internet. It may have some gaps, but it still works pretty well.
